questions.explanation: The first half of the test is a matter of description and the second is a matter of prediction, and that is the whole of the difficulty. A jury can look at a pamphlet and say whether it is of a kind that might produce refusal to comply; it cannot look at a pamphlet and say how many people will read it, what they will do on reading it, and how soon. A prediction of that kind can be made differently by different people from the same document, and a test whose operation depends on such a prediction will decide comparable cases differently, which is the property a good legal test is supposed to lack. The refinements that came later were all attempts to reduce the reliance on prediction, first by dropping the words about danger in favour of an insistence on the purpose of the speaker, and then by requiring that the advocacy be directed to inciting an imminent lawless action likely to occur. Imminence is still a prediction, and the difficulty has never been entirely removed.

questions.explanation: The arrangement separates two things that a reader is tempted to run together. The statute fixed the terms on which independence was to come, including a date and a period of transition, and it prescribed the content of a constitution for the place. It also gave the United States a say in whether that constitution was acceptable, and that say was about the constitution. The distinction is the one the item is about, and it matters because a condition on the constitution is a condition a people may be able to accept, whereas a condition on independence is a thing no constitution can reach. Whether the prescribed terms were a reasonable basis for a constitution is a separate question, and the strongest criticism of the statute is not about the conditionality but about the terms prescribed and the length of the transition, which those who governed the place at the time regarded as an evasion and those who negotiated it regarded as the only available arrangement.

questions.explanation: A declared interest is a standard, and its presence in a statute is a common way of making a set of conditions arguable rather than arbitrary. If the statute says the conditions are in the interest of the people of the place, then someone who objects to a condition can say the condition is not in their interest, and the argument has to be had in public on the subject rather than dismissed as a matter of discretion. The declaration does no work beyond that: it does not make anybody consent unnecessary, it does not accelerate the date the statute fixes, and it does not by itself give a person a thing to sue for. The other three options each treat a statement of purpose as though it were an operative provision, and the confusion is a familiar one, because a statute that mixes a statement of interest with a set of commands can easily be read as though the statement were one of the commands. answer.exemplar: A strong answer says the two accounts agree that the rule has persisted and disagree about whether the persistence is evidence of its soundness, since a rule that has stood is not thereby shown to have been decided rightly. It should notice that the first account has to explain why the question was open at all, and that the second has to explain why a court that thought the reasoning untenable nevertheless left the rule in place. questions.explanation: The disagreement is about what persistence proves, and it is the kind of disagreement that runs through a great deal of constitutional history. A rule that has been applied for a long time without being disturbed looks, from one side, like the best available answer to a question nobody has answered better, and the length of its life is part of the case for it. From the other side, a rule that has persisted because courts have preferred continuity to correction is a rule whose soundness has not been examined, and persistence is a fact about the courts rather than about the question. Neither account can be settled by counting the years, and the honest position is that the two are answering different questions about the same history: one about whether the question was open and has been answered acceptably, and one about why an answer nobody now accepts has not been replaced.

questions.explanation: An amendment that forbids something is a different kind of instrument from one that creates the machinery for the prohibition to work, and this amendment deliberately did only the first. It declared the prohibition, said the article should be inoperative unless ratified within a set period, said the prohibition should operate one year after ratification, and said that Congress and the several states should have concurrent power to enforce it by appropriate legislation. That last clause is the whole of the enforcement architecture, and the word doing the work is concurrent: it means that both the national and the state governments may act, and that neither is left to stand down. The amendment prescribed no penalty and no mode of enforcement, which is why the statute that supplied them was a matter of legislative choice and why the choice was contested. An account that reports the clause as supplying a penalty or a date has read the wrong sentence of the amendment, and both of those things were deliberately left to be settled later.

questions.explanation: A number in a statute is a policy choice and this one had an effect that the people who wrote the amendment did not necessarily intend. The amendment prohibited intoxicating liquors for beverage purposes without saying how strong a drink had to be, and the implementing statute answered that question with a line of one half of one per centum of alcohol by volume, which is far below the strength at which a drink is ordinarily called intoxicating. questions.explanation: The reasoning is one of silence plus a neighbouring text. The Constitution says that the number of representatives shall not be apportioned among the states according to their respective numbers, and the obvious use of that sentence is to attack the whole distribution of seats, so the state argued that it answered the objection to a district of twice the population. The decision answered that the sentence is about the allocation of seats among the states and says nothing about how the seats of a state are arranged within it, and then it found elsewhere in the text a requirement about the way a representative is chosen: a person chosen to represent a district is chosen by the people of the district, which presupposes that the districts are of a comparable size. The principle is therefore that a textual silence is not a prohibition, and that a court may take a requirement from one part of a text and apply it to a situation that another part has left open. That is a familiar enough technique in constitutional interpretation and an unusual one to see stated this plainly, which is why the case is read for its method as well as for its result.

questions.stem: A decision of 1964 is set out below in words composed for this bank, not taken from any historical text. It holds that where a state is divided into congressional districts of very different population, the votes cast in the more populous district have a different weight from those cast in the less populous, and that the constitutional requirement that the number of representatives shall not be apportioned among the states according to their numbers does not prevent the conclusion, since the requirement addressed the allocation among the states and not the arrangement of the representatives from each. What is the principle the decision rests on?

stimulus.body: Original document authored for this bank, not a historical text. From a decision of 1964, composed for this bank in the terms of the period: the objection that the number of representatives from a state ought to bear a relation to the number of its people, and that the whole arrangement of the seats is therefore fixed by one sentence of the Constitution, is disposed of by observing that the sentence in question provides that the number of representatives shall not be apportioned among the states according to their respective numbers, and that this is a direction as to the allocation of seats among the states. In the same section it is provided that the representatives shall be elected by the people of the several states, and by the people of the several districts which are to be apportioned among the states. A district in which the vote of a citizen is worth half the vote of a citizen in another district of the same state does not represent the people of that district in any sense in which the word is used in the text, and the arrangement complained of is therefore not sanctioned by the sentence relied on. We therefore hold that the population of a congressional district within a state is not required to be the same as the population of the other districts in that state, but the votes of the more populous district are not to be weighted more heavily than those of the less populous, and we remand the cause for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.

questions.explanation: The two decisions are read together constantly and it is worth being exact about why they were not the same decision twice. The congressional case turned on the text about electing representatives by the people of the several districts, and it turned on a silence in the sentence about apportionment among the states; the state legislature case turned on the guarantee of equal protection, which is a guarantee of a state and not merely a text about the mechanics of an election. That difference matters in two directions. It matters for the sources, because one decision had to find a requirement and the other had a guarantee to apply. It matters for the future, because a guarantee applied to a state legislature can be invoked by a person who is worse off than his fellows and can be applied to a state that has never drawn an equal district, whereas the requirement about electing by districts has to be found again in a different text if it is to be used about a different subject. That is why the two decisions are companions and not duplicates, and why a reader who merges them loses the part of the argument that came from the guarantee.

questions.explanation: A decision entered without an opinion of the court is a decision whose reasons are not the reasons of the court, and that is a distinctive and awkward position. The judgments bind as to the outcome; the reasoning that produced them does not, because no single account of the case commanded a majority, and so there is no authoritative statement of the ground on which the result rests. That is what makes such a decision a frequent starting point for later argument: a later court may accept the result, reject the result, or accept it on a ground that no justice in the earlier case suggested, and none of those is a departure from an established rule because there was no established rule. The second and third options both make the confusion that a decision without reasons is a decision without authority, and the fourth substitutes a rule of narrowest grounds for something quite different, since a narrowest-grounds rule is a way of choosing among reasons that exist and there were not enough agreed reasons to choose among.

answer.exemplar: A strong answer says the two accounts are not rival reports of the same event but rival claims about what a division of a decision accomplishes, since a court that answers some questions and not others has done a specific thing rather than nothing. It should notice that the first has to explain why a court that can answer part of a question does not answer the rest, and that the second has to explain why judgments were entered at all if the court did not know the answer. It should avoid presenting either as settled and avoid saying the second refutes the first, since a court that worked through part of a question can be both working and not knowing the rest.

questions.explanation: The two accounts are about the status of a partial answer. The first treats the division as the work: a statute that reaches both federal and state elections presents a single question with two limbs, and a court that decides the first and refuses the second has said something definite about both, and has identified the point at which the two lines part. On that account the absence of an agreed opinion is a matter of reasons rather than of results, and the results are what a later court must reckon with. The second treats the division as a confession, and it has the evident advantage that a court which does not know an answer should not pretend to. Its difficulty is that judgments were entered and results obtained, and the machinery of the country went on operating on them, so the account has to say what the results are worth if the court did not know how it got them. The useful position is probably that the two are answering different questions about the same episode, one about the decisional act and the other about the reasoning, and that the standing of the results and the standing of the reasons can come apart.

questions.explanation: The three steps ask three different questions and the distinction between them is what gives the test its shape. The first is about the purpose of the law, which is a question about the state of mind of the legislature and can be answered from what those who enacted it said. The second is about the principal effect of the law as it operates, which is a question about what a person encounters in fact. The third is about the relationship between church and state that the administration of the law produces, which is a question about entanglement. A test that asked only about purpose would let a law with a bad effect pass, and a test that asked only about effect would let a law with a religious purpose pass where the effect was small, and the three together are an attempt to catch both. What the test does not do is supply a definition of excessive entanglement, and that is the step which has been the hardest to apply, since the whole question is a matter of degree with no number in it.

questions.explanation: The passage is best read as a refusal of one metaphor and an acceptance of a problem. A wall implies a line with a definite place, and the decision says that is not the case, because some relationship between a government and religious bodies is unavoidable and the question is always about the degree and the kind. Once that is conceded, the work falls on the two questions that can be applied to a particular law: whether its principal effect advances or inhibits religion, and whether the administration of it entangles church and state beyond what is tolerable. Neither of those is a number, and both require a judgement, which is the difficulty the passage concedes without resolving. questions.explanation: The decision is remembered for a sentence about the wall, and the holding behind it is narrower than the sentence suggests. The programme was upheld, and the reasoning was that the state was not paying for religious instruction but for transportation, and that the instruction itself was given by the church and paid for by the church, and that the children were taken to the religious instruction and brought home again rather than being taught religion in the school. Two features of the arrangement carried the holding, and both are about arrangement rather than about motive: what the children were taken to do, and how the cost was divided. The decision did not hold that every arrangement of this kind is safe, and it did not lay down a test that could be applied to a different arrangement, which is part of why the field was unsettled for another quarter of a century. questions.explanation: The pair is a good example of a doctrine whose reach is settled case by case, and the second case is about the first rather than about employment. The first decision held that a programme of religious exercises made part of a public school programme by state authority could not stand, and it did so on a reasoning about what the state was requiring and about the effect on those who did not take part. What it did not do is say anything about a person who is not a pupil, and so the second decision had to ask whether the same reasoning disposed of a claim by an employee who had been dismissed for declining to join such a programme. The relationship between the two is therefore a question about the reach of the first, and the tension in the pair is precisely the difficulty of saying how far a rule about a state programme reaches a person who is not in the programme. answer.exemplar: A strong answer says a later reader has documents and knowledge that were not available to the court, so that what can now be shown about the grounds of the order is a different question from whether the court was entitled to accept the account put before it. It should notice that the dissent shows the ground was contested at the time and therefore not unargued, and it should avoid saying the later judgement shows what the court knew, since that is a claim about the interior of a decision nobody can now inspect.

questions.explanation: Two distinct questions are being confused in almost every argument about a decision taken in wartime. The first is what the court decided, and the lawfulness of the decision has to be assessed on the record as it stood, including what was placed before the court and what was withheld from it, and the materials that have since come to light are evidence about the second question rather than about the first. The second is whether the account on which the court proceeded was true, and that is a question the documents can now bear on, because the ground of the order is a matter of fact and fact is not a matter of what a court could have known. The dissent is important for a third reason, because it shows that the ground was contested inside the court at the time and not merely afterwards, so the later criticism is not a charge that nobody thought about it. A claim that a decision was wrong because it was decided on a false account of the facts is a very different claim from a claim that the court should have seen through the account, and only the first of them can be established by what has come to light since.
questions.hint: Ask what a later reader has that a court sitting in wartime did not, and what a later reader does not have.
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a later finding about the facts from a claim about the lawfulness of a decision

questions.explanation: Three point two divided by one half is 6.4, so the later line permitted a drink six and a half times as strong as the earlier one. Checked a second way, one half of one per centum is 0.5 and 0.5 multiplied by 6.4 is 3.2, the same relation checked in the other direction. The comparison is worth making because the two lines are both expressed as strengths and the effect of raising a line is not a change in the strength of any drink but a change in which drinks are inside the prohibition. The earlier line of one half of one per centum was far below anything anybody would call intoxicating, so beer and light wines were within it; the later line of three point two per centum took them out, and it did so by amending the enforcement statute rather than by touching the amendment, which is the whole of why the sequence in 1933 was possible. Each wrong answer is the value of a named slip: one half divided into three point two is 0.156 and so gives 0.16, and three point two added to one half is 3.7.

questions.explanation: A judgment construes a statute, and the force of the construction travels with the statute, so there is a real difference between a decision whose statute is still in force and one whose question has been answered by an amendment. What the amendment did was to supply by the slower route what the statute had attempted by the faster one, and the question the division had raised, which was how far Congress could go by statute, is no longer live in that form because the country has taken the other route. That is not the same as saying the judgment was wrong, and the third option is wrong for a reason worth stating: a judgment does not lose its force merely because a legislature has amended the statute, but the question it raised is a question about the reach of legislative power, and once the result is in the Constitution that question has been answered by a different instrument. The fourth option is the confusion to avoid, since a decision about a statute and a decision about an amendment answer different questions and one is not a precedent for the other.
questions.hint: Ask what instrument now supplies the result the statute had attempted, and what kind of question that puts out of reach.
questions.learningObjective: describe the standing of a statutory construction after the same result is placed in the Constitution
